newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Luxembourg sets out EU presidency programme.
newsitem.headline: Luxembourg sets out EU presidency programme.

text.p: Luxembourg began its six-month stint in the European Union driving seat in earnest on Thursday, laying out to visiting European commissioners an agenda that will focus on enlargement, monetary union and jobs.
"The Luxembourg presidency has plenty on its plate. It is well prepared and keen to cooperate with us," Commission President Jacques Santer told a news conference.

The main goal during Luxembourg's six-month stint is preparing the EU for expansion. Membership talks with central and eastern European applicants are due to start six months after the agreement of a new EU treaty, which was reached on June 17 at a summit in Amsterdam.
Santer said discussions should begin in early 1998.

On July 16 the European Commission is due to publish its recommendations on their readiness to join, and the presidency has the delicate task of working out the method by which the enlargement talks will proceed, and whether talks will begin with all or just some applicants.
Santer said not all candidate countries would be seen in the same light because of their varying sizes and economies.
"This examination will inevitably lead us to a differentiation between countries," he said.
At the same time, he said, there would be a proposal for a structure to allow those who were not in the first wave of enlargement to be "anchored" to the EU and to take part in certain programmes.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker added that the presidency did not intend "to send out a signal to those countries that might not be chosen for the first round of enlargement...that Europe is turning its back on them."

The presidency must also continue technical work on economic and monetary union (EMU) and ensure the timetable for Europe's planned single currency, the Euro, which its sees as the EU's "last big ambition this century", is not threatened by delay.

"The Commission and the presidency are convinced a single currency will be created on January 1, 1999. We want to ensure the convergence criteria are respected by the largest number," said Juncker, who is also the country's finance minister.

He said a "significant number" of countries were expected to take part in the euro launch on that date, and the presidency was not worried by "nervous debates" surrounding the single currency, though it was attentive to them.

With increasing demands for Europe to do more to fight unemployment, Luxembourg has also been given the task of holding a summit on jobs in the autumn, with November 22 now pencilled in as a possible date.
This gave more time to prepare than an October summit, as had been previously suggested, Santer said.
Juncker said it was important that the summit did not become a token gesture, and that it gave "added value".
He has already sent a letter this week to his European counterparts asking them to suggest experiences of fighting unemployment which have proved successful in their countries.
Replies were expected by the end of July, a Luxembourg official said.
